outline_section.section_title: Introduction to Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output
outline_section.learning_goal: Connect a computed convolution result to the output signal of an LTI system and preview the interpretation routine used throughout the lesson.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Create a compact LTI-system schema showing input x(t) entering a system labeled h(t), output y(t)=(x*h)(t), and small aligned time axes for x(t), h(t), and y(t) to reinforce that the convolution result is the output signal.
visual_elements: LTI system block with input arrow labeled x(t)
three small aligned time axes labeled input, impulse response, and output
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a simple black-and-white technical diagram; keep labels readable and avoid adding numeric signal data not specified by the tutorial writer.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Explicitly teach that once convolution has been computed, the piecewise function is interpreted as y(t), the time-domain output of the LTI system driven by x(t) with impulse response h(t).
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a finite-duration input and finite-duration impulse response whose convolution has already been computed as a simple piecewise output with one rise, one peak or plateau, and one fall.
paragraph_plan: State the LTI input-output relationship and remind the learner that h(t) characterizes the system.
Identify the convolution result as the output signal y(t), not as a separate object from the system response.
Describe the minimum interpretation routine: name y(t), read where it is zero or nonzero, locate breakpoints, and describe how the output changes across intervals.
Connect breakpoints to changes in overlap between x(tau) and h(t-tau), while emphasizing that this lesson interprets a result rather than recomputing the integral.
Preview that the examples will move from identifying y(t) to explaining the output behavior jointly from x(t) and h(t).
display_math_plan: Show a generic piecewise form for y(t) with zero regions outside a finite interval and nonzero formulas inside.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial short and schema-focused; do not rederive convolution bounds or evaluate integrals.

prompt_blocks.text: The plot shows the convolution output $y(t)$. State where $y(t)$ is nonzero, and state where $y(t)=0$.

question.correct_answer: $y(t)$ is nonzero for $-1<t<3$, and $y(t)=0$ for $t<-1$ and $t>3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the plotted curve as $y(t)$. The output leaves the zero line at $t=-1$ and returns to the zero line at $t=3$.
The endpoint convention is not the focus here; -1 and 3 are the support boundaries.

images.section_title: Connecting Piecewise Breakpoints to Changing Overlap
images.image_description: Create a clean black-and-white instructional diagram with four aligned panels. Panel 1: a fixed rectangular support for x(tau) on a tau-axis from tau=0 to tau=4. Panels 2-4: matching tau-axes showing the shifted support of h(t-tau) at t=p, t=q, and t=r, with overlap against x(tau) highlighted. At t=p, the right endpoint of h(t-tau) just touches the left endpoint of x(tau), so overlap begins. At t=q, the supports are exactly aligned with maximum overlap; highlight this panel. At t=r, the left endpoint of h(t-tau) just touches the right endpoint of x(tau), so overlap ends. Add a small y(t) plot at the bottom with breakpoints p, q, and r marked, and visually emphasize the breakpoint q.

outline_section.section_title: Connecting Piecewise Breakpoints to Changing Overlap
outline_section.learning_goal: Explain each breakpoint of a piecewise output as a time when the overlap relationship between x(tau) and h(t-tau) changes.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show aligned panels for x(tau), h(t-tau) at representative t values, and the resulting y(t) plot with breakpoints labeled so the learner can connect overlap changes to piecewise intervals.
visual_elements: shifted h(t-tau) support on matching tau-axes for several t values
output y(t) graph with corresponding breakpoints marked
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a small number of representative panels; the visual should reduce load by making overlap changes visible, not by redoing every convolution step.

question_policy.practice_question_model: A convolution output y(t) has a breakpoint at t=c. Which overlap change between x(tau) and h(t-tau) explains that breakpoint?
distractor_plan: Attribute the breakpoint to a change in amplitude with no support event.
Use the wrong endpoint of x(tau) or h(t-tau).
Confuse increasing overlap with decreasing overlap.
Describe a no-overlap event at a time when partial overlap still exists.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A finite-duration input and impulse response produce a piecewise output y(t) with breakpoints at t=a, t=b, and t=c. Explain what changes in the overlap between x(tau) and h(t-tau) at each breakpoint.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that piecewise boundaries in y(t) correspond to starts, endpoint crossings, or endings of overlap in the convolution integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds causal explanation for the support and interval boundaries rather than only reading them from y(t).
solution_step_plan: List the breakpoints in increasing order.
For each breakpoint, identify which endpoint of x(tau) or h(t-tau) aligns.
Describe whether overlap begins, changes growth pattern, changes shrink pattern, or ends.
Connect each overlap event to the matching piece of the output.
practice_variation_axes: Vary which endpoint alignment causes the middle breakpoint.
Use rectangular or triangular finite-duration signals.
Ask about one breakpoint at a time before combining all breakpoints.

outline_section.handoff_notes: The worked solution should interpret already-known breakpoints; do not make this a full overlap-bound derivation lesson.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a piecewise convolution output with breakpoints $p<q<r$. Which overlap change explains the breakpoint at $t=q$?

choice_blocks.text: The shifted support first touches the support of $x(\tau)$, so overlap begins.
The supports reach maximum alignment, so the overlap changes from growing to shrinking.
The shifted support has moved completely past $x(\tau)$, so overlap ends.
Only the height of $h(t-\tau)$ changes; the support overlap stays the same.
The supports still partially overlap, but the output should be treated as zero.

question.correct_answer: The supports reach maximum alignment at $t=q$, so the overlap changes from growing to shrinking.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A breakpoint marks a support event in the convolution overlap. At $t=q$, the supports are aligned at maximum overlap, so after q the overlap no longer grows in the same way.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: t=q:\quad \text{overlap changes from growing to shrinking}

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a piecewise convolution output with breakpoints $a<b<c$. Which overlap change explains the breakpoint at $t=c$?

choice_blocks.text: The shifted support first touches $x(\tau)$, so overlap begins.
The supports reach an interior alignment, so overlap changes pattern while remaining nonzero.
The shifted support reaches its last contact with $x(\tau)$, so after this time no overlap remains.
Only the amplitude of $x(\tau)$ changes; no support endpoint event occurs.
The overlap is increasing at $t=c$, so the output has just turned on.

question.correct_answer: At $t=c$, the shifted support reaches its last contact with $x(\tau)$, so the overlap ends.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: At the last breakpoint, the moving support has reached its final contact with the fixed support. After that point, the two supports no longer overlap, so the output returns to zero.

outline_section.section_title: Explaining Output Shape from the Input and Impulse Response
outline_section.learning_goal: Relate the rise, plateau, fall, or curvature of y(t) to how the input and impulse response overlap over time.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show x(t), h(t), and the resulting y(t) on aligned time axes, with the output shape divided into labeled intervals such as rising, constant, and falling.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use simple finite-duration signals; avoid visually dense plots and keep the shape explanation tied to overlap amount or weighted overlap.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given plots of x(t), h(t), and the resulting y(t), which explanation best accounts for why y(t) rises, levels off, and then falls over the labeled intervals?
distractor_plan: Explain the output shape using x(t) alone.
Explain the output shape using h(t) alone.
Reverse the interval order of rise and fall.
Ignore weighted overlap and describe only endpoint locations.

choice_blocks.text: The output has that shape because $x(t)$ is wide; $h(t)$ does not affect the rise, level part, or fall.

question.correct_answer: The output rises as overlap increases, stays level while the overlap amount is constant, and falls as overlap decreases.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shape of $y(t)$ comes from the joint overlap in the convolution integral, not from either signal alone. More overlap gives the rising segment, constant full overlap gives the level segment, and shrinking overlap gives the falling segment.

question.correct_answer: The output rises while the weighted overlap with larger values of $x(\tau)$ grows, then falls after that weighted overlap shrinks.

prompt_blocks.text: A piecewise convolution output $y(t)$ for an LTI system is shown. Which summary correctly describes the system output?

choice_blocks.text: For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before p and after s, nonzero on $p<t<s$, rises on $p<t<q$, stays level on $q<t<r$, and falls on $r<t<s$.
For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before p and nonzero after p; the graph only shows where the response starts.
For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ rises on $p<t<q$, falls on $q<t<r$, and stays level on $r<t<s$.
The plot summarizes $h(t)$: the impulse response rises, stays level, and falls between p and s.
The LTI system will always have this same output shape for any input because the breakpoints are system properties.

question.correct_answer: For this input and impulse response, $y(t)$ is zero before p and after s, nonzero on $p<t<s$, rises on $p<t<q$, stays level on $q<t<r$, and falls on $r<t<s$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A complete output summary names the zero regions, the nonzero support, the breakpoints, and the behavior inside each nonzero interval. It must also describe the response for the given input and impulse response, not $h(t)$ alone or a system property independent of input.
